original_value: The complex interplay of a number of physical and meteorological phenomena makes simulating clouds a challenging and open research problem. We explore a physically accurate model for simulating clouds and the dynamics of their transitions. We propose first-principle formulations for computing buoyancy and air pressure that allow us to simulate the variations of atmospheric density and varying temperature gradients. Our simulation allows us to model various cloud types, such as cumulus, stratus, and stratoscumulus, and their realistic formations caused by changes in the atmosphere. Moreover, we are able to simulate large-scale cloud super cells - clusters of cumulonimbus formations - that are commonly present during thunderstorms. To enable the efficient exploration of these stormscapes, we propose a lightweight set of high-level parameters that allow us to intuitively explore cloud formations and dynamics. Our method allows us to simulate cloud formations of up to about 20 km × 20 km extents at interactive rates. We explore the capabilities of physically accurate and yet interactive cloud simulations by showing numerous examples and by coupling our model with atmosphere measurements of real-time weather services to simulate cloud formations in the now. Finally, we quantitatively assess our model with cloud fraction profiles, a common measure for comparing cloud types.

result.paraphrase: The complex interaction of multiple physical and meteorological phenomena makes cloud simulation a difficult and still open research problem. We present a physically accurate approach for simulating clouds and how they transition. Using first-principles formulations for buoyancy and air pressure, we can simulate atmospheric density variations and changing temperature gradients. The simulation supports a range of cloud types, including cumulus, stratus, and stratoscumulus, along with realistic cloud formation driven by atmospheric change. In addition, we can model large-scale cloud supercells—clusters of cumulonimbus formations—commonly seen during thunderstorms. To make these stormscapes easy to explore efficiently, we introduce a lightweight set of high-level parameters for intuitive control of cloud forms and dynamics. Our method can simulate cloud formations spanning up to about 20 km × 20 km at interactive rates. We demonstrate the capabilities of physically based yet interactive cloud simulation with many examples and by combining our model with real-time weather-service atmosphere measurements to generate cloud formations in the now. Finally, we evaluate the model quantitatively using cloud fraction profiles, a standard measure for comparing cloud types.
